content:
Your church's federal income-tax exemption does not settle its state sales-tax or property-tax treatment. Before claiming relief on a purchase or a worship space, check the rules for that tax with the agency that administers it.

Use this guide to prepare those questions and the supporting paperwork. The state examples illustrate differences, rather than provide rules you can carry into another state.

---

## Start with the federal distinction

A church that meets section 501(c)(3) requirements is automatically exempt from federal income tax without applying for IRS recognition. That federal rule concerns income tax. Check state purchase exemptions and property exemptions separately.

| Question | Where to begin |
|---|---|
| Does the church qualify for federal income-tax exemption? | IRS church guidance and section 501(c)(3) requirements. |
| Can the church buy an item without sales or use tax? | Your state's tax agency and its rules for the transaction. |
| Does a particular property qualify for exemption? | The office administering property exemptions where the property is located. |

<Callout type="important">
Tax guidance checked October 16, 2026. Before relying on an exemption, confirm current eligibility, application forms, filing dates and continuing requirements with your state tax agency and the local property-tax office. The examples below name the Texas Comptroller, California Department of Tax and Fee Administration, and California State Board of Equalization.
</Callout>

---

## Find the right offices

The Federation of Tax Administrators maintains a directory called "Tax Agencies" that takes you to state tax-agency websites. The IRS also has a "State Links" directory with information for tax-exempt organizations.

Use your state's agency site to find its religious-organization guidance. For property, check who receives the claim. In California, county assessors administer the Church and Religious Exemptions; a sales-tax application is a different process.

Prepare separate questions about purchase eligibility, supplier documentation, property eligibility and filing requirements. Use the relevant agency's instructions to answer each question rather than treating "tax-exempt" as a complete answer.

---

## Check whether purchases qualify

Texas offers an application route for qualifying nonprofit religious organizations. Its religious category requires an established group regularly meeting at a designated location for worship. Federal exemption is not required for that category, but the group must apply for the state exemption.

California has no comparable broad sales-and-use-tax exemption for nonprofit and religious organizations. Specific exemptions and exclusions exist, so check the actual transaction before claiming relief.

Ask your own agency whether your church and proposed purchase qualify. If the agency offers a religious category, read its definition before choosing it. A religious purpose alone does not establish eligibility under every category, as the Texas guidance explains.

---

## Gather the application evidence

Use the application for the exemption category you are claiming. For example, Texas Form AP-209 is its application for religious organizations.

The form's independent-church option requests a statement of faith, the regular order of worship, evidence that services are open to the public and how they are advertised, and a description of the worship facility. Its affiliated-church option instead asks for evidence of the qualifying parent relationship.

Treat those as examples of activity evidence, not a nationwide document checklist. Read the instructions that apply to your church's structure and affiliation. Supply the supporting information the application requests.

<Callout type="tip">
Build your application file from the agency's own checklist. Texas AP-209 warns that applications received without supporting documentation will be returned. Check the attachments before sending yours.
</Callout>

---

## Use an approved exemption correctly

Approval and purchase documentation are separate steps. In Texas, an approved organization documents a qualifying purchase by giving the seller a completed exemption certificate. The exemption-certification side of Form 01-339 is distinct from its resale-certificate side.

Texas requires exempt purchases to relate to the organization's exempt purpose. Personal purchases by employees or volunteers do not qualify, even when the organization reimburses them. Check the purpose of the purchase before using church exemption paperwork.

<Callout type="warning">
A purchase exemption does not settle tax on items your church sells. The Texas Comptroller says exempt organizations must collect tax on most sales of taxable items. Check the sales rules before a fundraiser or merchandise sale.
</Callout>

---

## Check the property's ownership and use

Ask the property-tax office which exemption fits the property and its actual use. Describe who owns or leases it and what happens there.

California's Church Exemption can apply to property owned, leased or rented by a religious organization and used exclusively for religious worship services. Its separate Religious Exemption concerns qualifying church-owned property used for religious purposes. Use the correct category rather than assuming the names are interchangeable.

If you rent, ask about the lease as well as the claim. California's Church Exemption guidance says a qualifying reduction on leased property must benefit the church. Ask the assessor how the ownership and use of your proposed space affect eligibility.

---

## Confirm filing dates and continuing eligibility

Ask the administering office for the initial filing date and any later claim or eligibility-confirmation requirements. Check the specific exemption you receive.

In California, the Church Exemption requires an annual claim. The Religious Exemption has a one-time claim, but claimants receive an annual form to confirm continued eligibility. A one-time application does not mean you can ignore that later form.

California's Religious Exemption remains effective until terminated or the property is no longer eligible. Check with the assessor when ownership or activities change rather than relying only on the original approval.

---

## Keep the evidence with your records

IRS church guidance calls for records that support exemption and document receipts and expenses. Keep the evidence behind your claim and the transactions recorded in your books.

Use this filing checklist as an organizing suggestion:

- [ ] Keep the submitted application and its supporting documents together.
- [ ] Add the agency's decision and the instructions for using it.
- [ ] File purchase invoices and receipts with the relevant accounting records.
- [ ] Keep property records with the evidence of qualifying ownership and use.
- [ ] Add later claims and eligibility confirmations to the same file.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s."* — Mark 12:17 (LSB)
</Callout>

claim_check.notes: Writer checked all listed originals on 2026-10-16; independent Opus sentence, scripture and screenshot review remains required. Application and certificate PDFs were opened directly with urllib and read with pdftotext when the web tool could not retrieve them. Practical prompts and the records checklist are editorial applications of the cited agency instructions, not additional legal duties.

rulings: Texas and California are limited illustrations, not a state-by-state rules list. No rates, thresholds, filing-date numbers, processing promises or savings estimates are stated.
Filing checklist is an organizing suggestion, not a prescribed format or retention schedule.
No theology, pastoral-care or methodology decision is made. Required scripture uses the same checked Mark 12:17 direct-speech excerpt as the published federal-exemption article.
